variants.text: The eroded remains of a volcano near Coonabarabran, and Australia's first Dark Sky Park.
Volcanic spires and unpolluted night skies in the Warrumbungle Range, 550 km north-west of Sydney.
A National Heritage-listed volcanic range where the Breadknife rises 90 m from the valley floor.

Warrumbungle National Park covers 23,311 ha of the Warrumbungle Range, the eroded remnant of a volcano near Coonabarabran, about 550 km north-west of Sydney. Walkers come for formations such as Belougery Spire, Crater Bluff and the Breadknife, which towers 90 m above the valley floor and is the park's most recognisable feature. The volcanic landforms were added to the National Heritage List in 2006, and in 2016 the park became Australia's first certified Dark Sky Park. About 80% of it burned in January 2013, and walking tracks, campgrounds and visitor sites have since been rebuilt.

The Warrumbungle Range is what remains of an ancient volcano, reserved as a national park in 1953 and covering 23,311 ha near Coonabarabran. Its spires and bluffs, among them Belougery Spire, Bluff Mountain and Mount Exmouth (the tallest peak), were National Heritage listed in 2006 for volcanic landforms described as unrivalled in Australia. Siding Spring Observatory sits on the park's eastern edge, and the International Dark-Sky Association certified the park itself on 4 July 2016. There is no food for sale inside, so visitors bring their own.

Rising out of the plains about 550 km north-west of Sydney, the Warrumbungles are the weathered core of a volcano, with 23,311 ha protected as a national park. Day walkers head for the Breadknife and Grand High Tops, while others come to camp under skies the park's managers describe as having zero light pollution. Siding Spring Observatory, opened in 1965, stands on the park boundary partly because of those dark skies. The sealed road in from Coonabarabran is about 30 km.

tips.text: Entry is $8 per vehicle per day, and the park can close for poor weather or fire danger, so check NPWS alerts before driving out.
Siding Spring Observatory is open to visitors by day only, 8:30 am-4 pm; for night viewing book a Coonabarabran Stargazing tour.
No food is sold in the park, so bring water, a hat, sunscreen and food, and borrow a free locator beacon at the visitor centre for the High Tops loop.
Allow 5-6 hours for the Grade 4 High Tops loop, or take the 12.5 km return via the Dagda Shortcut.
Summers often top 30C and winter nights drop below freezing, so pack for the season.
The observatory closes on extreme fire-danger days, and caravans cannot use its narrow access road.
The sealed road from Coonabarabran is about 30 km; the west approach via Coonamble has unsealed sections.
The visitor centre is open 9am-4pm daily except Christmas Day and sells star charts.
Siding Spring's cafe and Exploratory are closed on Tuesdays, though the AAT Visitor Gallery opens seven days.

spots.name: Breadknife and Grand High Tops Walk

bio_variants.text: A 14.5 km Grade 4 loop from Pincham car park, climbing past Belougery Spire and Crater Bluff to the Grand High Tops and views of Bluff Mountain.
The park's signature walk, following Spirey Creek to the 90 m Breadknife and the volcanic peaks of the High Tops, with a shorter 12.5 km return via the Dagda Shortcut.
A day-long loop to the Breadknife and the Grand High Tops, with spring wildflowers and wedge-tailed eagles along the way.

spots.name: Siding Spring Observatory

bio_variants.text: A working research observatory on Mt Woorut, opened in 1965 on the park's eastern edge, with a public Exploratory, a cafe and the AAT Visitor Gallery open by day.
Telescopes on the 1160 m Mt Woorut, built beside the park partly for its dark skies, with a daytime visitor gallery, cafe and Exploratory.
A research observatory at the end of Observatory Road that welcomes visitors by day only; night viewing is through a Coonabarabran Stargazing tour.
